Skewness and Kurtosis Tests of Model Fit

Source: R/skew_kurtosis.R
skew_kurtosis_test.Rd

Checks whether a fitted mixture of normal distributions reproduces the skewness and kurtosis of the data. A mixture of normals can be skewed and heavy-tailed overall, through the spread of its classes; what it cannot produce is a shape its classes do not add up to. A data set whose shape the fitted model does not reproduce is evidence that the number of classes, or the normality of the outcomes within each class, is wrong (Muthén, 2003).

Each statistic is computed on the data and on nsim data sets simulated from the fitted model; the simulated values give the statistic's distribution under the model, and the p-value is two-sided: twice the smaller of the shares of simulated values at or above, and at or below, the sample value.

The fitted parameters are estimates, not known values, and that uncertainty belongs in the reference distribution. Each simulated data set is therefore generated from its own parameter draw, taken from the normal approximation to the estimates' sampling distribution (centred on the estimates, with the inverse of the observed information as its covariance, on a scale where variances are log standard deviations and class sizes log-ratios), with classes drawn from the drawn class sizes and the estimation sample size. Holding the parameters at the estimates instead understates the spread of the skewness statistics markedly, because a mixture's skewness moves with the separation and sizes of its classes, which are the least precisely estimated parts of the model; the kurtosis statistics are dominated by sampling noise and change little.

Usage

skew_kurtosis_test(fit, nsim = 100, seed = NULL)

Arguments

fit

A model with continuous outcomes from fit_gmm(), fit_lcga() or fit_mixture(), fitted to complete data.

nsim

Number of simulated data sets.

seed

NULL, or an integer for the simulation; a supplied seed leaves the caller's random number state as it was.

Value

A list of class "skew_kurtosis_test" with data frames multivariate, univariate and bivariate, each with columns statistic ("skewness" or "kurtosis"), the variable(s), sample, mean, sd and p_value.

Details

The statistics, for complete data:

  • univariate: the skewness \(m_3 / s^3\) and the excess kurtosis \(m_4 / s^4 - 3\) of each outcome, \(m_r\) its \(r\)-th central sample moment and \(s^2\) its sample variance on \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom;

  • bivariate and multivariate: Mardia's (1970) skewness \(b_{1,p} = n^{-2} \sum_{i,j} (d_i^\top S^{-1} d_j)^3\) and kurtosis \(b_{2,p} = n^{-1} \sum_i (d_i^\top S^{-1} d_i)^2\) of each pair of outcomes and of all of them, \(d_i\) the centred case and \(S\) the covariance matrix on \(n\) degrees of freedom. Under multivariate normality \(b_{2,p}\) is about \(p(p + 2)\).

The p-values carry the simulation's own noise; with the default 100 data sets they are good to about two decimals.

References

Mardia, K. V. (1970). Measures of multivariate skewness and kurtosis with applications. Biometrika, 57(3), 519-530.

Muthén, B. (2003). Statistical and substantive checking in growth mixture modeling: Comment on Bauer and Curran (2003). Psychological Methods, 8(3), 369-377.

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1)
n <- 300
cls <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
y <- outer(ifelse(cls == 1, 3, 1), rep(1, 4)) +
  outer(ifelse(cls == 1, 1, 0.2), 0:3) + matrix(rnorm(n * 4, 0, 0.7), n, 4)
fit <- fit_gmm(y, n_classes = 2, times = 4, random_effects = "none",
               n_init = 3, random_state = 1)
skew_kurtosis_test(fit, nsim = 20, seed = 1)
